source_text: Verum ut urgeamus locum: constitit nempe iniustitiam Deo adhaerere non posse, constitit etiam ab ipso esse praescriptum, ne obsint filiis peccata generantium; asseruit quidem ipsa praecipientis dignitas iniustum id esse quod prohibet. Porro, ut agamus tecum liberalius, respondendi tribuo facultatem de his duabus opinionibus, quas supra comminus posui, id est ut imputentur peccata parentum filiis vel non imputentur; quam putas credi iustitiam debere? Si dixeris tuam quam vis etiam ultimo convenire iudicio, refero, utrum illam, quae remansit, nostram iustam an iniustam putes: sine dubio iniquam pronuntiabis; at haec legis auctoritate custodienda mandatur. Vides ergo unum remanere necessario de tribus: ut aut legem Dei fatearis iniustam, immo per legem Deum ipsum iniquitatis accuses aut certe ad vocem confugias magistrorum tuorum et dicas legem, quae per Moysen data est, a Deo tuo non fuisse mandatam, aut, si hoc utrumque proferre non audes, traducem peccati asseri contra legis documenta et praecepta fatearis. Neque enim adeo te desipere posse credendum est, ut dicas Deum iustitiam quidem in praeceptis, in iudiciis vero iniquitatem tenere aut certe secundum dogma vestrum in iudiciis quidem servare iustitiam, praeceptis autem iniquitatem do cere; quod licet superius egerimus, nunc tamen necessario repetivimus.
pass_a_gloss: But that we may urge the place: it has stood, surely, that injustice cannot cling to God; it has also stood that it was prescribed by him that the sins of those generating not harm sons; the dignity of the precepting one himself has asserted that that which he forbids is unjust. Further, that we may deal more liberally with you, I grant the faculty of answering concerning these two opinions which I placed face to face above, that is that parents' sins be imputed to sons or not be imputed; which justice do you think ought to be believed? If you have said yours which you want even the last judgment to convene with, I refer whether you think that which has remained, ours, just or unjust: without doubt you will pronounce it unfair; but this is commanded by the authority of the law to be kept. You see therefore that one of three necessarily remains: that either you confess the law of God unjust, nay through the law accuse God himself of injustice, or certainly take refuge in the voice of your teachers and say that the law which was given through Moses was not commanded by your god, or, if you dare to bring forth neither, you confess that a vine-layer of sin is asserted against the documents and precepts of the law. For it is not to be believed that you can be so foolish as to say that God holds justice indeed in precepts, but iniquity in judgments, or certainly according to your dogma that in judgments he keeps justice but in precepts teaches iniquity; which although we have treated above, we have nevertheless now necessarily repeated.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: But let us press the point. It has been established that injustice cannot belong to God. It has also been established that he himself commanded that parents’ sins must not harm their children. The dignity of the one giving the command itself declared unjust what he forbids. Yet, to deal more generously with you, I give you the opportunity to answer. Of the two opinions I just placed face to face—parents’ sins should be charged to children, or should not be charged to them—which do you think should be regarded as just?

If you say your own, which you want applied even at the final judgment, I ask in turn whether you regard the remaining opinion, ours, as just or unjust. You will undoubtedly pronounce it unfair. But the law’s authority commands this very position to be maintained. You see, then, that one of three alternatives necessarily remains. Either you admit that God’s law is unjust—indeed, through the law, accuse God himself of injustice—or you resort to your teachers’ language and say that the law given through Moses was not commanded by your god. Or, if you dare say neither, you must admit that inherited sin is asserted against the law’s teaching and commands. Surely we cannot believe you capable of such madness as saying that God maintains justice in his commands but injustice in his judgments—or, according to your doctrine, justice in his judgments but teaches injustice in his commands. Although we dealt with this above, it was necessary to repeat it now (Deuteronomy 24:16).

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
